design_detail: Two-page Viewpoint (JAMA Psychiatry; read as the online-first PDF, published online 4 November 2020, pages E1-E2) that sets three hypotheses for the cannabis-schizophrenia association (1, entirely causal; 2, partly causal and partly confounded by genetic or familial effects and/or reverse causation; 3, entirely non-causal), states in a Table what each of four genetically informed methods should show under each hypothesis (discordant-relative or co-relative designs, Mendelian randomization, linkage disequilibrium score regression, polygenic risk score regression) and compares the expectations with published results. Nine references; no search, no new data.
can_establish: How two authors from a psychiatric and behavioral genetics institute, one of whom co-wrote the only co-relative study they cite, read the genetically informed evidence available in 2020, and what pattern of results they expect each method to give under each hypothesis.
cannot_establish: What proportion of the association is causal: the quantitative statement (familial confounding accounting for more than half) rests on one co-relative study (a Swedish national registry study by its title as cited by Gage et al., 2016, and as Ksir and Hart, 2016, describe it; the viewpoint says neither) whose monozygotic-twin estimate is printed two ways and was not significance-tested, and the viewpoint has no systematic search.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (viewpoint). The co-relative study is a Swedish national co-relative registry analysis (Giordano et al. 2015; the viewpoint does not describe it, and its design is taken from the reference lists and text of Gage et al. 2016 and Ksir and Hart 2016); the other studies are genome-wide association analyses and polygenic-score studies in population samples, as cited.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated beyond the four methods; studies of the short-term psychiatric effects of administering cannabis are explicitly out of scope (p. E1).
sample.selection_effects: The authors know of only one discordant-relative analysis, co-written by Kendler; three of the four large population-based polygenic-score studies said to be positive are not cited; non-genetic designs (cohorts, dose-response, potency) are outside the question asked.

exposure.measurement: By method, as cited: cannabis misuse in the co-relative study, a national registry study by its title (cannabis abuse in its title); genetic instruments for lifetime cannabis use in the Mendelian randomization studies, which the authors note are not instruments for heavy use or misuse; lifetime cannabis use or misuse in the genetic-correlation studies; cannabis misuse and other cannabis phenotypes as outcomes of schizophrenia polygenic scores.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not addressed; the Mendelian randomization evidence concerns liability to lifetime use only.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed, except that high schizophrenia polygenic scores are said to predict comorbid substance use or misuse as well as cannabis use (pp. E1-E2).

comparison.controls: Co-relative design: the association in unrelated pairs from the general population compared with that within full-sibling pairs and monozygotic twin pairs discordant for cannabis misuse. Mendelian randomization: people with higher versus lower genetic liability to the exposure.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Within-pair comparisons remove familial factors shared by relatives, but not factors that differ between them (childhood adversity affecting one twin, prodromal symptoms before the first registry record of misuse); not discussed in the viewpoint.

outcomes.instruments: Schizophrenia as a registry diagnosis (co-relative study) or as case status in genome-wide association studies; cannabis phenotypes as outcomes in polygenic-score and reverse-direction Mendelian randomization analyses.
outcomes.operationalization: The hypotheses are defined by expected patterns (Table): under 1, equal odds ratios across levels of relatedness, a genetic correlation of zero and a schizophrenia polygenic-score coefficient of zero; under 2, odds ratios that fall with relatedness but stay significantly above 1 in monozygotic twins, and coefficients above zero; under 3, odds ratios falling to 1 in monozygotic twins and no effect of liability to cannabis use in Mendelian randomization.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited, with the primary source of each. Co-relative (Giordano et al. 2015): OR 10.44 for unrelated pairs in the general population, 5.07 for full siblings, and for discordant monozygotic twins 3.52 in the text (a 66% decline) or 3.92 in the Table; tests of significance were unavailable for monozygotic pairs. Mendelian randomization: genetic liability to lifetime cannabis use increased schizophrenia risk by 37% (Vaucher et al. 2018); much stronger evidence that genetic liability to schizophrenia increases lifetime cannabis use (Gage et al. 2017; Pasman et al. 2018); no evidence of pleiotropy for the instruments in all three. Genetic correlation between lifetime cannabis use or misuse and schizophrenia 0.22 to 0.25 (two studies). Polygenic scores: no association with cannabis misuse in one restricted sample (Hjorthoj et al. 2019); high schizophrenia scores predicted more cannabis and comorbid substance use in four large population-based studies, one cited (Verweij et al. 2017), effect sizes small and not given. Editors' calculation from the printed odds ratios: the 66% decline is on the odds-ratio scale; on the log scale the odds ratio falls by 46% (with 3.52) or 42% (with 3.92), and the excess odds (OR minus 1) by 73% or 69%.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only one of the four positive population-based polygenic-score studies is cited; the effect sizes of the polygenic scores, the unit behind the 37% Mendelian randomization estimate and the numbers of discordant monozygotic pairs are not given.
analysis.power: Not addressed beyond the remark that the number of available studies is modest (p. E2).

interpretation_gap.results_show: One co-relative study (a Swedish national registry study by its cited title) shows the odds ratio for cannabis misuse and schizophrenia falling from 10.44 in unrelated pairs to 5.07 in full siblings and to about 3.5 to 3.9 in discordant monozygotic twins, without a significance test at that level. Of three Mendelian randomization studies, one estimates an effect of liability to lifetime cannabis use on schizophrenia and two find stronger evidence for the reverse direction. Genetic correlations are modest (0.22 to 0.25) and polygenic-score effects small.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusions say there is relatively reliable evidence across methods that the association stems partly from shared familial or genetic risk and/or reverse causation, good evidence against an entirely non-causal association, and that in the one co-relative study familial confounding "accounts for more than half of the observed association" (p. E2). Gaps: (1) the more-than-half statement rests on one co-relative study (a registry study by its cited title) co-written by Kendler, holds on the odds-ratio and excess-odds scales but not on the log scale on which odds ratios are modelled (a 46% or 42% fall; editors' calculation), and uses a monozygotic estimate printed as 3.52 in the text and 3.92 in the Table; (2) by the viewpoint's own criterion, separating hypothesis 2 from 3 in this design requires a monozygotic odds ratio significantly above 1, which was not tested (Table, footnote e), so the evidence against hypothesis 3 rests mainly on one Mendelian randomization estimate; (3) the Table expects a genetic correlation of zero under an entirely causal model, but a causal effect of cannabis use on schizophrenia would itself make variants that influence cannabis use associate with schizophrenia, so a correlation above zero does not by itself show confounding (editors' appraisal; the same applies, less strongly, to the polygenic-score expectation); (4) measurement error in the exposure attenuates within-pair estimates more than population estimates, which would make a co-relative decline overstate confounding; not discussed (editors' appraisal). The closing warning that claims about changing risk with changing use are very likely exaggerated is limited by the authors to estimates without control for confounders, and the prudent conclusion (some causal effect, an appreciable non-causal share) is in line with the evidence they present.

timeline.event: Giordano et al., Swedish national co-relative control study (Kendler co-author): the only discordant-relative analysis cited, the basis of the more-than-half estimate. Ksir and Hart (2016) cite the same study as showing that most of the association disappears after controlling for familial relationships; Gage et al. (2016) read it as showing that population estimates may be overestimated.
Marconi et al., meta-analysis of the association between level of cannabis use and psychosis, cited for the robust association.
Gage, Hickman and Zammit had proposed Mendelian randomization as a way to minimise confounding, then limited by the lack of genetic variants robustly predicting cannabis use.

Ksir and Hart argue for shared vulnerability, reading the same co-relative study, an Australian twin and polygenic-score study (Power et al. 2014) and a US family study as strong evidence for shared vulnerability over a causal contribution.

Gage et al., two-sample Mendelian randomization: much stronger evidence that genetic liability to schizophrenia raises lifetime cannabis use than the reverse. Verweij et al.: genetic correlation and polygenic-score association between schizophrenia and cannabis use.

Vaucher et al., Mendelian randomization: genetic liability to lifetime cannabis use associated with a 37% increase in schizophrenia risk. Pasman et al., genome-wide study of lifetime cannabis use with genetic correlation and Mendelian randomization pointing to a causal influence of schizophrenia liability on cannabis use.

Di Forti et al., EU-GEI study of the contribution of cannabis use to variation in the incidence of psychotic disorder across Europe, cited for the robust association. Hjorthoj et al.: no association between genetic liability for schizophrenia and cannabis use disorder in a restricted sample.

This viewpoint, published online 4 November 2020 (print issue 2021); the authors call for further co-relative and Mendelian randomization designs and for controlled pre-post studies of schizophrenia incidence where cannabis use rose after decriminalization.

replication.where_it_stands: The clearest short statement of the partly-causal reading from genetically informed designs. Its quantitative core is one co-relative study; the Mendelian randomization results are mixed (one estimate of an effect of liability to cannabis use, two of the reverse direction, all with instruments for lifetime rather than heavy use). Claims citing it should name the primary studies, give the co-relative odds ratios with their scale, and not present more than half as a measured proportion.

funding.funder: Not reported (the viewpoint has no funding statement).
funding.declared_conflicts: Conflict of Interest Disclosures: none reported (Article Information, p. E2).
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors: Virginia Institute for Psychiatric and Behavior Genetics, Department of Psychiatry, Virginia Commonwealth University; Gillespie also QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute, Australia. Kendler is an author of the only co-relative study cited (Giordano et al. 2015), on which the more-than-half statement rests. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the viewpoint.

what_would_settle_it: Co-relative analyses in several registries with exposure recorded before any prodromal symptoms, reporting the numbers of discordant monozygotic and sibling pairs and confidence intervals at each level of relatedness, combined with Mendelian randomization that uses instruments for heavy use or cannabis use disorder and methods robust to pleiotropy; and the controlled pre-post studies of schizophrenia incidence the authors propose.

domains.note: No search or criteria; the authors cite the studies they know of, and three of the four positive polygenic-score studies are not cited.

Some limitations are named (Mendelian randomization instruments for lifetime use only; a restricted sample in the null polygenic-score study; no significance test for monozygotic pairs), but not the co-relative design's sensitivity to measurement error and to non-shared confounders, nor the number of discordant pairs.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The only co-relative study, which carries the quantitative conclusion, is co-written by Kendler.

The more-than-half statement is presented as what the study suggests but depends on the scale and on an untested, inconsistently printed estimate; the expectation of zero genetic correlation under causation is asserted without justification; good evidence against hypothesis 3 is stronger than the evidence shown.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for causal and non-causal explanations
domains.note: Results pointing both ways are reported (an effect of liability to cannabis use; a monozygotic odds ratio above 1), but limitations that would bias the genetically informed designs towards finding confounding are not discussed. Under-represented: the weaknesses of the designs favoured by the viewpoint.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a viewpoint or narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the overall judgment follows the worst domain, the absence of a systematic search. The viewpoint is short, explicit about its hypotheses and expectations, and hedged in its conclusion, but its single quantitative claim rests on one study by one of its authors, printed inconsistently and not significance-tested at the decisive level. It may be cited for the framework (what each design should show under each hypothesis) and as a pointer to the co-relative and Mendelian randomization studies; the numbers belong to those primary studies.

key_findings.finding: Framing: cohort studies and meta-analyses show a robust association of cannabis use, heavy use and misuse with later schizophrenia, but adjusted models cannot determine how much is causal; for prevention, the causal proportion is critical. Three hypotheses are tested against four genetic methods (two natural experiments, discordant-relative designs and Mendelian randomization, and two measures of genetic association, genetic correlation by LD score regression and polygenic risk scores). Confounding means genetic risks raising both cannabis use and schizophrenia; reverse causality means schizophrenia liability or symptoms raising cannabis use. Short-term effects of cannabis administration are out of scope.
key_findings.page: p. E1 of the online-first PDF

key_findings.finding: Co-relative evidence: only one analysis is known (Giordano et al.). Schizophrenia was significantly increased among people with cannabis misuse, but the odds ratio fell as genetic relatedness increased, from 10.44 in the general population to 3.52 for discordant monozygotic twin pairs, a 66% decline, which the authors read as consistent with hypothesis 2 (partly causal, partly confounded) and as suggesting substantial confounding.
key_findings.page: p. E1 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.note: Exposure: cannabis misuse (the cited study's title says cannabis abuse); outcome: schizophrenia. The viewpoint does not say what the population estimate was adjusted for, or how many discordant pairs there were. The Table gives a different monozygotic value (see reporting issues). Editors' cross-check and calculation: the Table (p. E2) gives 3.92; 66% matches 3.52; the log odds ratio falls by 46% (3.52) or 42% (3.92), and the excess odds by 73% or 69%.

key_findings.finding: Table summary of published results: discordant pairs, OR 10.44 for unrelated pairs, 5.07 for full siblings and 3.92 for monozygotic twins, consistent with hypothesis 2; Mendelian randomization, stronger evidence of reverse causality, consistent with hypothesis 2; genetic correlation 0.22 to 0.25 (modest pleiotropy) and schizophrenia polygenic scores predicting several cannabis phenotypes, each consistent with hypotheses 2 and 3. Footnotes: tests of significance were unavailable for monozygotic twin pairs; all 3 Mendelian randomization studies found no evidence of pleiotropy for their instruments.
key_findings.page: p. E2 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Table, Summary of published results and Results consistent with rows; footnotes e and f

key_findings.finding: Mendelian randomization: using genetic variants as instruments, Vaucher et al. found that genetic liability to lifetime cannabis use was associated with a 37% increase in schizophrenia risk; Gage et al. and Pasman et al. found much stronger evidence that genetic liability to schizophrenia increased lifetime cannabis use (reverse causality). The instruments are associated with lifetime use, not heavy use or misuse. In aggregate the authors judge the results most consistent with hypothesis 2.
key_findings.page: p. E1 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.note: The viewpoint does not state the unit of genetic liability behind the 37%; take it from the primary study (ref. 1, Vaucher et al.).

key_findings.finding: Measures of genetic association: the authors state that a genetic correlation or schizophrenia polygenic-score coefficient above zero is incompatible with an entirely causal association, while neither method can distinguish hypothesis 2 from 3. Two LD score regression studies reported significant genetic correlations of 0.22 to 0.25 between lifetime cannabis use or misuse and schizophrenia. One polygenic-score study, in a restricted sample, found no effect on cannabis misuse; four large population-based studies, including Verweij et al., found that high schizophrenia scores predicted more cannabis and comorbid substance use or misuse. Despite modest correlations and small effects, the authors conclude these show significant confounding inconsistent with hypothesis 1.
key_findings.page: pp. E1-E2 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Measures of Genetic Association, 1st paragraph (p. E1, continued on p. E2)

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: across the 4 methods, with considerable but not complete consistency, the findings argue against an entirely causal association; despite a modest number of studies, the evidence that the association stems partly from shared familial or genetic risk and/or reverse causation is called relatively reliable, and the evidence against an entirely non-causal association good; the 1 co-relative study suggests familial confounding is substantial and accounts for more than half of the association; genetic correlation and polygenic-score results suggest more modest confounding and raise the possibility of reverse causation. Prudent conclusion: some causal effect of cannabis on schizophrenia risk is possible, while an appreciable part of the association is not causal; claims about changing schizophrenia risk with changing cannabis use that are based on population associations without control for confounders are very likely exaggerated. Further co-relative and Mendelian randomization studies are needed, and controlled pre-post designs of schizophrenia incidence in states where cannabis use rose with decriminalization.
key_findings.page: p. E2 of the online-first PDF

reporting_issues.issue: The monozygotic-twin odds ratio from the co-relative study is 3.52 in the text (p. E1), where the 66% decline is computed, and 3.92 in the Table (p. E2).
reporting_issues.page: pp. E1-E2 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two values is wrong; the decline would be 62.5% with 3.92 (editors' calculation). Take the value from Giordano et al. (2015) before quoting either.

reporting_issues.issue: The Table's Mendelian randomization cell cites refs 5 to 7, but ref. 7 (Hjorthoj et al.) is described in the text as the polygenic-score study that found no effect; footnote f refers to all 3 Mendelian randomization studies, which in the text are refs 1, 5 and 6.
reporting_issues.page: pp. E1-E2 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: Citation error in the Table; the reverse-causation Mendelian randomization evidence is refs 5 and 6, and ref. 1 is the study supporting an effect of cannabis-use liability.

reporting_issues.issue: Of the four large population-based polygenic-score studies said to show that schizophrenia scores predict cannabis use, only one (Verweij et al., ref. 8) is cited.
reporting_issues.page: p. E1 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: Three of the studies behind the polygenic-score conclusion cannot be identified from the viewpoint.
